module

public import Mathlib
public import FormalConjecturesForMathlib.Data.Nat.Prime.Composite

open scoped Nat

@[expose] public section

/-!
# Carmichael Numbers

*References:*
 - [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carmichael_number)
-/

/--
A Carmichael number is a composite number `n` such that for all `b ≥ 1`,
we have `b^n ≡ b (mod n)`.
-/
def IsCarmichael (n : ℕ) : Prop :=
  ∀ b ≥ 1, n.Coprime b → n.FermatPsp b

reformulations.difference: The definition embeds compositeness in a universally quantified Fermat-pseudoprime condition and tests only positive coprime natural bases using exponent n−1. The docstring and Wikipedia instead describe composite n satisfying b^n ≡ b modulo n for all bases.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: Taking b=1 forces ¬n.Prime and 1<n through Nat.FermatPsp. For b≥1, Nat.probablePrime_iff_modEq converts the natural-number divisibility condition to b^(n−1) ≡ 1, without truncated-subtraction artifacts. A coprime base cannot be zero once n>1. Korselt's criterion and Fermat's theorem modulo each prime factor give the all-base congruence; conversely, cancellation of a coprime base gives the exponent-(n−1) condition. Integer bases reduce to natural residues. Scratch proofs establish equivalence both with the exact docstring and with Wikipedia's all-integer-base definition, for every n : ℕ.

reformulations.difference: The count uses Set.ncard of all natural Carmichael numbers satisfying n≤x, without explicitly restricting n to the interval [1,x].
reformulations.equivalence_argument: IsCarmichael n implies 1<n, so the omitted lower bound is automatic. The underlying set is contained in the finite natural interval Iic (Nat.ceil x), so Set.ncard's infinite-set default is unreachable. Scratch proofs establish equality with the intended interval-restricted set, finiteness for every real x, zero count for x≤1, and positive count for x≥561.

reformulations.difference: The source's C(x)=x^(1−o(1)) is represented by log(C(x))/log(x) tending to 1.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: Eventually x>1 and C(x)>0. Set ε(x)=1−log(C(x))/log(x). The stated limit is precisely ε(x)→0, and exponentiation gives C(x)=x^(1−ε(x)). Conversely, taking logarithms of that representation gives the limit. Also C(x)≤x eventually, so ε can be nonnegative if that convention for 1−o(1) is intended.

reformulations.difference: The source's exponential asymptotic is expressed as convergence of a normalized logarithm to 1.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: For sufficiently large x, put A(x)=log(x)·log(log(log(x)))/log(log(x)), which is positive. The Lean expression is exactly −log(C(x)/x)/A(x). Its convergence to 1 is equivalent to C(x)=x·exp(−(1+ε(x))A(x)) for some ε(x)→0, by taking logarithms or exponentiating. Positivity of C(x) on the relevant tail excludes logarithm default-value issues.

sources_consulted: J. D. Lichtman, Primes in arithmetic progressions to large moduli and shifted primes without large prime factors, arXiv:2211.09641, introduction and Carmichael-number corollary; LaTeX source from https://arxiv.org/e-print/2211.09641

review.notes: No mathematical defects found in the sole library definition or its IsCarmichael-dependent use sites. Mathlib's similarly named carmichael is the reduced totient function, not a duplicate predicate. The separate OeisA309132.IsCarmichaelNumber predicate was also proved equivalent. /workspace/review/scratch.lean compiles successfully; the equivalence and counting proofs have no sorryAx dependencies. Boundary tests exclude 0, 1, primes, 4, 9, and 341. A proved finite decision procedure computes exactly [561, 1105, 1729] up to 2000. No repository source files were edited.
